Now that was an agreement! It was a settlement reached by two responsible governments after negotiations in an attempt to determine the needs in each region of Quebec, Mr. Speaker. I took part in these negotiations personally and I can say that many members of the Quebec caucus worked hard on these issues and held many meetings with farmers from all areas to ascertain their needs, to understand them and be able to meet those needs adequately through a procedure and a program approved by Quebec and its producers.
I received yesterday a letter of thanks from the president of the APU, the Agricultural Producers' Union of three great regions, Quebec East, Quebec West and Quebec Centre. This letter, which I received this morning at my office, thanks me personally and the Quebec Members who are interested in agriculture for having worked with the agricultural producers. This was not achieved after 20 years, but after six months. We worked at it, we came to an agreement and some $30 million have been spent in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, another important issue was resolved a few weeks ago, that of assistance to sugar beet producers. On April 18, the Government announced-

-that it would provide assistance of up to $8 million, or $10 per standard tonne, to sugar beet producers in Alberta, Manitoba and Quebec in co-operation with the provincial Governments of those provinces. Since that time agreements have been reached with Manitoba and Quebec, but Alberta producers will not be growing sugar beets this year.
[ Translation]
We made an agreement with sugar beet producers. We were made aware of this issue. We sat with them, we thought it over, and agreements were reached. Some negociations are still going on. We are still experiencing difficulties with one of the provinces, but all the same we went to bat for our farmers who were struggling against serious difficulties. I think it is important to realize what has been achieved in that area, Mr. Speaker. We knew that sugar beet producers all across the country were in trouble because of poor foreign market conditions, and we supported them. That is not hot air. Those are facts, concrete facts for anyone to see.

I will now turn to the subject of the Ontario Veterinary College animal pathology lab. When the Minister of Agriculture was in Guelph on April 29 he announced that the federal Government would contribute $6.5 million to match funds provided by the provincial Government for the renovation of
the Ontario Veterinary College. He also announced the construction of a $5 million animal pathology laboratory at the University of Guelph, which will not only serve area livestock producers, but will also be used in the training of students. Through numerous federal-provincial agricultural agreements the federal Government is helping to develop the unique production and marketing potentials of every region of Canada.
In the interest of time I won't go into the details of those programs. I would, however, like to mention some clear examples of the Government's respect for the authority and the talents of Members of this House in response to the false accusations made in the Member's motion.

It is not true, Mr. Speaker, to say that we did not further economic development, especially in agriculture. This is one sector where it cannot be said. I think no one in this House has the right to suggest that we have done nothing to further economic development in agriculture. Agricultural issues were raised more than 70 times since September, and I think it is important that we let the people hear about it or that, wherever they are, they read about it in Hansard tomorrow. I hope they do so that they know what really goes on.

Following up on our election campaign promise to take action in regard to Section 31 of the Income Tax Act, the capital gains tax on farm land and the possibility of establishing an agri-bond program to facilitate farm credit. On February 25 the Minister of Finance instructed the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to hold hearings on the three tax issues. The Committee's report was presented early last month.
I hope the Opposition Parties will agree with me that the Committee's observations and recommendations vividly demonstrated the value of Parliamentary study of a pressing issue. All concerned parties had an opportunity to present their views on the three subjects and the Members of Parliament on the Committee were as straightforward in their analysis of the situation as they were bold in their recommendations. [Translation]
We have not left this issue up in the air. We were committed to consider these matters during the election campaign but one cannot simply snap one's fingers and table legislation without giving it some consideration and without consulting the Canadian people. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I, for one, have sat with Members of my party to consult groups and associations throughout the country, the people of Canada, who were anxious to be consulted, Mr. Speaker. When you have not been consulted for twenty years, you are pleased to see Ministers and Government Members sitting down with the people to ask them what they want, what their real interests and their expectations are, and to be able to discuss with them on how to achieve those expectations after giving the matter some consideration and assessing the impact. Now is not the
May 14, 1985

time to engage in extravagant expenditures and end up with a accumulated deficit of $226 billion, as we now have. We cannot be expected, Mr. Speaker, and I think it is important, to introduce programs here and there and everywhere. We must be good managers. This is why the youth have elected us last September 4. They have made a harsh judgment on the previous Government, and they told us: We have trusted you, go and put your house in order, and that is what we have been doing since September, Mr. Speaker. It is not an easy task and it will take some time. We need the confidence of the people, as well as the good will of all parties, including the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party. Given the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think that we are now in a position, after eight months in office, to present an interesting picture to the people that shows how seriously we have taken the fiscal problems of the Government.
Questions or comments. Debate. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak in support of the principle of this motion. I have listened carefully to speeches by Hon. Members today. I think it is fair to say that in the past Liberals have accomplished some good things for agriculture, although I could not find too many examples.
Name one.

Surely if one is in power for 40 years something good must take place sometime, somewhere and somehow. While I am unable clearly to identify any, indeed there have been some rather minor assistance packages for the farm sector.
Let me open my remarks by referring to what has happened in my constituency in the last three weeks. I come from a constituency where agriculture plays a very major role. There are 1,200 full-time farms and a number of part-time and hobby farms.
I notice that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) is in the House. We are still awaiting for that clarification with respect to how the tax system affects part time farmers. That clarification was promised before the election, during the election and after the election-it has been eight months. I simply want to flag that for the Minister in the hope that we will have that clarification in the near future with respect to how the tax system affects this critical area.
Three weeks ago I spoke to a sheep rancher in my constituency. He is from a large sheep farm that has operated for three generations. His grandfather had settled in the area and commenced a large sheep operation. He took over this operation from his father and I believe his son will look forward to taking over this family operation. I say this merely to point out that this case does not involve an overnight introduction of
Supply
sheep ranching into the area but indeed an operation that has lasted for three generations.
This distraught sheep rancher came to me to say that the production costs of raising sheep on his ranch were far higher than the prices he was receiving for his animals. In short, he was saying that it is no longer profitable to run a sheep ranch in central British Columbia, no matter what the size of the ranch. Furthermore, he was using the most modern methods and sophisticated management techniques. He suggested that three generations of sheep ranching was about to end unless the federal Government could assist him. He asked if I believed that the federal Government could assist him by implementing measures to assist the farm sector in a real way.
I am always honest with my constituents and therefore had to answer no. While I hope the federal Government would do so, it was my honest opinion, based on information I had at the time, that it likely would not. Of course, this was not encouraging to my constituent.
Later that week I talked to some 40 cattlemen in my constituency. They also told me that their cost of producing cattle was higher than the prices they were receiving and therefore they could not continue any longer. It is impossible in a cattle ranching area of western Canada to continue such an operation, despite the most modern equipment and sophisticated management techniques. These are very learned food producers who simply cannot continue without some support from the Government.
They told me that they had heard of a proposed red meat stabilization bill and asked if such a bill would solve the problem. I said that it would not solve the problem because if such a bill were passed the price that beef producers would obtain would be an average of the prices which I have just stated are too low to cover the costs.
Until the Government recognizes the value of the family farm in agriculture and that those people must obtain a fair price that is reflected in the cost of their operation, we will not have family farm operations in Canada. It will be replaced by agri-business and corporations. A very efficient way of food production will be removed from the agricultural landscape of Canada.
I met another individual in my riding who, along with others, was introducing a rabbit operation; they would raise rabbits, slaughter and sell them. He asked me if there was any federal support for such a venture and I advised him that he could receive assistance through the IRDP. He indicated that those running the IRDP were not interested in supporting such a venture. They did not have any faith in this type of food production and would not provide assistance. This is another clear signal that people in my constituency are receiving from the federal Government.
I was also approached by a number of people who were becoming involved in the potato producing sector. They had approached the federal Government for assistance in developing a processing storage facility. They were simply asking for assistance to begin operations and were quite prepared to repay the loan. However, when they made their inquiries to the

May 14, 1985
Supply
various Departments there was no money for this type of development.
I am beginning to sound like a broken record, but the point is that after all the assurances from the new Government, food producers in my constituency are telling me they cannot make a living and continue their operations. I think these human stories and tragedies that are unfolding speak for themselves.
I am asking Government Members to take these concerns seriously because there is a sense of disappointment in our constituencies. On behalf of our constituents in the food producing sector, we are appealing to the Government to introduce policies that will enable agriculture to continue in this country in a viable way.
During the election, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in my constituency that his Party had a whole set of solutions to agricultural problems. Agri-bonds was one solution, but these will not be introduced any longer. The Conservative Party said it would change the tax laws to allow many deductions that are not presently available. However, there is no indication that this will happen.
The Conservatives said they would bring in legislation, such as the United States Farm Home Administration Program, that will allow people to deal with these large debts they have accumulated. We have heard no discussion about such a proposal.
The Government said it could introduce a bill immediately that would assist hard pressed farmers and ranchers. It is called the Farm Creditors Arrangements Act. That legislation has been left off the list.
There has been no indication that the Government appreciates the plight of the agricultural sector. As a matter of fact, in many cases the Government is turning its back on food producers of this country.
We heard the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Kelle-her) stand in his place today and allude to the fact that the Government had a great idea that would allow tens of millions of pounds of heavily subsidized beef from Europe to be imported into the country in order to undersell all the Canadian beef producers. That is almost as ludicrous as when the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), talking about industrial policy, announced that he had great news for the House. He said that Mitel, a world leader in telecommunications technology and the second largest telecommunications company in Canada that is extremely well respected on the international stage would be sold to a foreign company. All the Members on the Government side applauded for some 15 or 20 seconds at this good news. It is a pathetic day when Parliament applauds the Minister responsible for developing industry in this country for saying the best news he has is that one of our best companies has been sold to a foreigner, and that technology that we as taxpayers-tens of millions of dollars by the way-will now be drained out of the country and taken advantage of by a foreign corporation. That is the good news. If that is the good news, Mr. Speaker, what
on earth is the bad news we are about to receive as people warn us of the up-coming Budget.
This motion before us today suggests that we ought to condemn the Government because a number of its policies regarding Crown corporations have not been developed properly. I listened to the Hon. Member across the way talking about things the Government has done to assist the food producers. There is one Bill I am waiting to receive in the House of Commons and to hear Members opposite debate it; that is the Bill to do away with Canagrex. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) said: "Listen, at a time when we are trying to expand into new markets and trying to provide economic opportunities for our food producers to sell their wares overseas, we have a good idea. We are going to scrap the Crown corporation that does this". Again there was some applause on the Government benches when the Minister stated that Canagrex is history now.
In the first few months Canagrex operated millions and millions of dollars of sales were organized overseas to assist our farmers. I asked the Parliamentary Secretary about it. Here was a Crown corporation set up to assist the farmers in Quebec, Ontario, in western and eastern Canada and it was doing an excellent job. I have not read a single report that said Canagrex was not performing beyong the wildest expectations that people had for that Crown corporation. But the Government is going to torpedo it and wrap it up. As a matter of fact, the Government already has.
When you consider what is going on today, Mr. Speaker, and when we hear from the Government that it has done certain things to assist farmers, let us recognize that the situation in the country is growing worse. Let us measure what is going on in terms of farm bankruptcies, and I am not certain this is the most appropriate way to measure the health of the agricultural sector, but it must be one way. When you look at the record going back to 1979, there were 125 farm bankruptcies in Canada. In 1980 there were 222; in 1981 there were 261; in 1982 there were 410; in 1983 there were 488; and in 1984 there were 551. In 1985, if you extrapolate the number we have today, there are over 600. Over the last five years, in every single year farm bankruptcies have increased in the country. This is surely only a tip of the iceberg when you consider all of those people who are walking away from their farms, price collapses and so on.
Look at the debt the farm community was facing in 1979. Total farm debt was $14.6 billion at an average interest rate of 11.6 per cent. In 1981 that amount had increased to $18.5 billion with an interest rate of 15.46 per cent. Today farm debt is in excess of $20 billion and increasing. I do not know how you would measure the health of the agricultural sector of our country. The only way we have before us would indicate that things are deteriorating and the situation is worsening. Now is the time to call for extraordinary measures on behalf of the federal Government to show the leadership necessary to provide an environment for this sector to develop properly.
May 14, 1985

What can be done? I listened to the Hon. Member with all due respect-I mean that-when he talked about Farm Credit, the tinkering and how this was helping farmers. The number of farmers that were helped is minuscule and the way they were helped by lowering debt a couple of percentage points is hardly the kind of leadership we were expecting from the Government. I think the tinkering and adjusting of the Farm Credit rate is at best a good joke. It is no solution.
What we need to do is look to our financial institutions. On November 7 last year I remember opening up The Globe and Mail and finding on one side this great, huge headline, "Financial Woes Assail Farmers". That is expected under present conditions. On the other page of The Globe and Mail it said, "Bank Profits in Canada the World's best". While the farmers of this country were literally being driven to their knees, the banks of Canada were identified as the most profitable banks in the entire world. Therein lies part of the problem. It is time we looked to our bankers and said, it is time they shared in this dilemma. Why are their profits up substantially while the farming sector is being crushed as a result of these high interest rates? Some of the European countries asked their banking communities to recognize the value of the family farm. They said to them, why not have interest rates for 25 years at say 8 per cent for the family farm?
Who is going to pay for it?

The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) just said: "Who is going to pay for it?" I will tell you who is going to pay for it, Mr. Speaker. The banks will. Because their profits have been some of the strongest in history, and because the Canadian interest rate spread is the largest and widest in the world, I think it is time Members of Parliament, including the nice fellow from Western Arctic, asked themselves why Canada has to tolerate the widest interest rate spread in the world. We go on to ask, is what is good for the banks good for everybody? It is not, Mr. Speaker. It is certainly not good for the farmers. I think it is time for the banks to carry their share of business and to stop foreclosing prematurely on some of these ranches and farmers as they struggle back into position.
How can this be done, Mr. Speaker? If the Government across the way had the guts and the commitment to help, farmers having difficulties in whatever part of Canada, it would introduce right now the Farm Creditors Arrangement Act 1985 which would allow relief to those hard-pressed farmers. When people ask, what can we do, that is one thing. We can look to the banks and expect them to share. We can introduce measures such as the Farm Creditors Arrangement Act that was introduced in the late 1930s and 1940s. It helped a lot of farmers at that time. Or we can look to our colleagues in the United States, in particular, the United States Farmers Home Administration. We could say that we will set aside without interest for five years as much as 25 per cent of debt owed by farmers in distress up to a maximum of $200,000; that the private lender is willing to write down a portion of
Supply
loans, and to reschedule repayment obligations one could apply to the FHA for a guarantee of the remaining outstanding debt of up to $400,000 for operating credit and $300,000 for real estate.
This is not a radical program. This is in place in the United States. Again as an example of what can be done, there it is. There are many things that can be done. I refer to the work done by the National Farmers' Union in the last few weeks as they have been visiting the various caucuses, laying out a variety of proposals that would assist the farm sector.
In closing I want to say that I do hope the Government gives some consideration to the point in this motion we are debating today on decentralization. Decentralization is an opportunity for Canadians in their own communities to solve their own problems. There is a great deal of interest in the idea of people getting on to solve their own difficulties and not waiting for the Government or for large corporations to do it, particularly foreign corporations. What about giving people an opportunity? We could assist local areas to develop food processing plants, assist in the development of food storage facilities and so on to allow potential food producers to develop lands that are presently not in development. Again, there are a variety of things the Government can do. Let us hope it has heard the points made today, and that a week from Thursday when the Budget is introduced all of these suggestions are included therein.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the Hon. Member talk of the tip re the iceberg referring to farm bankruptcies. If this is the tip of the iceberg, I think that the bottom of the iceberg would be to have an NDP government in office in Canada. Such is not the case, and I hope it never is.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that we agree to listen to the opinions of the Canadian people and of the Opposition on the problems we face in agriculture, but we had to wait for almost half an hour this afternoon for a single Opposition member to show up so that the Standing Committee on Agriculture could sit to study credits earmarked for agriculture, and officials from everywhere were kept waiting. If the Hon. Members wants to put up the farm sector policies of countries that have been led by social democratic Governments-every one of those countries-which are extremely viable, I will put them up against the Canadian experience any day of the week.

Mr. Speaker, in closing the debate today on this motion, I want to pay particular attention to that part concerning the activity or lack of activity of Crown corporations, and the role they can play in re-energizing the Canadian economy. I make mention of Canadian National and a number of its subsidiaries, whether it be CN Marine, Ports Canada or a host of other subsidiaries. I bring to the attention of the House that the role that these Crown corporations are playing or not playing is crucial to the poorer regions of this country.
I made mention before, as did the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau), of the cut-backs in ferry service by the Bluenose from Yarmouth to Bar Harbour. Members on the government side, particularly the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), find this to be no big deal. However, in that area of the country, particularly in that area of the Province of Nova Scotia, it is a very serious matter. In fact, the Premier of our province travelled to Ottawa to speak specifically to the Minister of Transport about this very important issue.
This gives ample evidence that this Government in its so-called desire to create economic wealth in this country has allowed these Crown corporations to abandon the responsibilities to those areas of the country which are perhaps in greatest need. The stalling tactics of the Minister of Transport to give us a positive decision with regard to changing that policy in Yarmouth is absolutely appalling to the people of Nova Scotia. It is a repudiation of the provincial Government, the provincial Tory MLAs, and certainly a repudiation and a shot in the face to the Hon. Member for South West Nova who has been attempting, as I have, to have this ferry service restored.
Another issue of great concern, which I believe the Opposition motion covers quite well, is the request made by the Maritime Farmers' Council. The Minister responsible sat in
his office and received briefs, delegations and representations from the provincial Premiers and Members of Parliament on all sides. He has elected to do nothing for the maritimes farmers. The request for emergency funding in the amount of $9 million has not even been answered.
The list goes on. It does not stop there. We recently heard that the European Economic Community may take action in terms of imports of various goods. This Minister has refused to send able negotiators there to represent the best interests of Canada. The beef industry is allegedly going to receive a slap in the face. Further importation of beef will be allowed into the Canadian market. I realize that some tough stands have to be made in order to represent Canadian interests. I find the stalling tactics used by the various Ministers not to be acting in the best interests of the Canadian economy.
What about Canagrex? That Crown corporation was set up to benefit the farming community in this country. Without any consultation whatsoever it was slashed. The operative word during the Throne Speech was "consultation". We found that the substance contained in the economic statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in November 1984 was not "consultation", but "cut, cut, cut". Canagrex has gone. So much for assisting the farming community in Canada.
The New Democratic Party Member referred to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion as the optimist. He stood in his place today and bragged about the agreements he had concluded with provincial Governments. I think he referred to 19 agreements. He failed to mention that the ones that he concluded in Newfoundland were concluded during the provincial election. Most of the background of those agreements was well in place before this Government took office.
The Minister bragged about the agreements he has signed in Nova Scotia. The Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. McMillan) is travelling across this country seeking greater input from Canadians with regard to tourism and additional moneys from the Canadian Government to further the aims of his portfolio. He finds that they have given a meagre $14 million to an entire province for tourism. I say shame! That will not cover one region of the Province of Nova Scotia.
The Minister failed to mention in any debate the agreements that he has not concluded with provincial Governments. This Minister is dragging his feet with regard to the SYSCO modernization plans, an agreement concluded in writing by the provincial Government of Nova Scotia and the Government of Canada. The Minister responsible is refusing to live up to his part of the agreement. The rationale has never been explained in this House or to the Canadian people. We only hear the Minister say they might review it, or they are going to review it. Meanwhile, hundreds of jobs are being put in jeopardy.
I could go on, but let me conclude with two points regarding decentralization. The decentralization of offices and services from areas which do not really need them to other areas of this country has been terminated by the Government. Of course, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is an economic

REGIONAL ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT-NOVA SCOTIA-CAPE BRETON COAL RESOURCES. (B) FEDERAL FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I put a question to the Minsiter of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) on May 8, and 1 was somewhat surprised by his answer. He said that money was approved for the further opening of a tunnel at the Donkin Mine. Since that time, statements have been made by the Chairman of the Board of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, as well as by the President, indicating that no money has been approved. The press secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion is not aware of any money being approved for the opening of new tunnels to new coal mines in Cape Breton. There has been absolutely no such approval. Such a request is before the Treasury Board in Cabinet, but the Minister quite conveniently said to the House, and to you, Sir, that the expenditure of this money had been approved. I am not suggesting that the Minister intentionally misled the House, but there are certainly some very strong arguments to suggest that one could conclude that that happened.
Notwithstanding the Minsiter's comments, I am afraid that his answer is not satisfactory. We in industrial Cape Breton want a clear commitment on the part of the Government of Canada with regard to new and expanded coal developments in that area of Canada. I remind the Parliamentary Secretary that the energy policy, both in spririt and in substance, is based primarily upon the utilization of Cape Breton coal. That is the fundamental policy thurst of the Conservative Government of Nova Soctia.
The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion has an obligation to the provincial Government of Nova Scotia. He has an obligation to those coal mining communities that depend in large part on the viability and future of those coal mines for jobs, for economic wealth and for job opportunities for their families. For the Minister to give no commitment to the Nova
Adjournment Debate
Scotia Government and the people of that area is, in my view, and abdication of his responsibilities as a Minister of the Crown, and it is an outright repudiation of a Tory Premier, John Buchanan.
Before a large audience in industrial Cape Breton the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) clearly spelled out that he was committed to coal and steel. I suggest that when commitments are made by politicians, particularly those who go on to become the Prime Minister of Canada, they ought to be lived up to. This Prime Minister is allowing his Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion to allow a particular resource industry in my province to go on without a firm commitment from the Government of Canada.
It is fine and dandy for the Minister to tell us that Devco has made a profit for the first time in "X" number of years. But, the fact is that the Minister had nothing to do with that. The present President had nothing to do with that. It was well in place before the Government assumed power. It is an irrelevant point. It is particularly odd that the Minister stood in his place and told us that Devco had made a profit, but could not tell us what the profit was because the statements had not been audited. I find that very misleading; or, I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it could be argued as being misleading.
Why does the Minister not come clean and tell us the answers? I will tell the House why. It is because this Government has said no to the Government of Nova Scotia with regard to future coal developments on the Island of Cape Breton. The Government has said no to the mining communities in those areas. It will not put additional moneys into the coal industry. The Government will flirt with some research moneys, but it will not continue assisting with new coal developments in Cape Breton.
The Minister said that the company has broken a promise. A total of 1,200 miners are walking the street as a result of the lack of commitment by the national Government. It is not only unfair in terms of regional development policy, it flies in the face of everything which the Prime Minister has allegedly tried to do in terms of co-operation with both levels of Government. It is not going ahead.
Two things could have happened. The Government of Nova Scotia could have backed off on its request for additional moneys for coal development in Glace Bay-and I would like to hear the Parliamentary Secretary zero in on that-or the Prime Minister could have given a directive to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion to change the mandate of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, and to run it like a business, because the Government would not provide further dollars for coal developments. I say that is a sick energy policy by a sick Minister, with a sick Prime Minister and a sick Government.

speechtext:
I think you could at least have listened to what the Minister said today and last May 3 as well.
When it comes to federal-provincial co-operation, it is a fact indeed that co-operation between this Government and the provinces, including Nova Scotia did improve.
Last April 30, the Minister of Energy and Mines of Nova Scotia, the president of the Cape Breton Development Corporation and the new chairman of the board of the corporation got together to discuss mining development projects, the corporation's production and the market outlook.
Mr. Matheson stated that better corporation management had put Nova Scotia's coal industry in a better position than it had known for years. He was pleased to learn that production and productivity have improved at Lingan Mine and Prince Mine. The unions full co-operation was an important factor. Mr. Matheson also welcomed the fact that coal production facilities will be able to meet the increasing needs of the Nova Scotia Power Corporation.
This press release shows evidence of the co-operation that exists between the federal government and the Government of Nova Scotia concerning coal and energy policies, and the development of coal resources in the province. Besides it was agreed that the Cape Breton Development Corporation and the Nova Scotia government would meet on a quarterly basis to discuss matters related to this industry.
As was mentioned by the opposition member, the profits of the Corporation are under review. The financial data for the current fiscal year are being gathered and examined by external auditors.
For the preceding fiscal year, ending on March 31, 1984, the Corporation had declared $49.6 million in operating losses. The Corporation intends to allocate 10 per cent of its operating profits to its Coal Division employees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-CHILD TAX CREDIT-TREATMENT IN NEWFOUNDLAND. (B) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext: That's a cheap shot.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-CHILD TAX CREDIT-TREATMENT IN NEWFOUNDLAND. (B) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It is clear from the comments of my colleague from Nova Scotia that this Government is ignoring eastern Canada. That is one of the reasons for my request tonight to speak on the issue of the refusal of the Minister to act on the Newfoundland Government's total abuse of the tax credit system as it affects single parents, particularly those people who need the money the most.
You will no doubt recall, Mr. Speaker, that Hon. Members on this side of the House were incensed to discover that the Government of Newfoundland was using the federal tax credits to gouge money from single parents; people like Shirley Parsons who could not even pay her electric bill because the money she was receiving as a single parent was insufficient. She went to the welfare department to ask for help. This was not a lolly-gagging layabout. This woman had a part-time job and she was seeking full-time employment in a province where the level of unemployment is higher than anywhere in Canada. She was supporting a family and she needed some help with her electric bill. Before the Newfoundland Government would give her help to pay the bill for the utility, which is in fact contracted for by the Newfoundland Government, it forced her to sign a statement to the effect that she would turn over her federal child tax credit to the Government.
When we raised this issue in the House, the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare denied any knowledge of such a request. He denied any knowledge of the fact that the Newfoundland Government was intent on squeezing blood from a stone. The Minister, instead of embarking on a nationwide study to see whether this type of practice is being followed by other provinces, washed his hands of the whole situation and said it did not exist.
I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the Newfoundland Government could not take the political heat, and in the few days leading up to the elections in Newfoundland it went to Mrs. Parsons and said, "We will pay your heating bill. We will pay you everything as long as you keep your mouth shut". But I must say that this woman had the courage of her convictions. She laid it out before the public. She told the Newfoundland Government that she was not speaking just on her own behalf, but on behalf of literally thousands of other people, primarily women and single parents, who find themselves in the position of being unable to pay the exorbitant charges inflicted on them by the Newfoundland Power and Light Company.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the federal Minister chose to ignore his responsibility to ensure that the child tax credits are not used by provincial Governments to extract dollars from
May 14, 1985

single parents and needy individuals. The purpose of the child tax credit from the very beginning was to assist those people who need help the most. It is clear that the Newfoundland Government's policy, which was stated in documents distributed in welfare offices across the province, was a clear violation of the spirit of the child tax credit as enacted by former Liberal federal Governments.
Notwithstanding the statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare about how they were going to preserve universality, preserve the child tax credit, did he use this opportunity to send a clear message to the provinces? Did he use this opportunity to say no, you are not going to touch that money because it belongs to Shirley Parsons and all of those single parents who are out there struggling to make ends meet? Did he lay down the law and tell Brian Peckford and the Newfoundland Conservatives that they were not going to pay the provincial heating bills on the backs of poor single parents? No, he washed his hands of the issue and said it was not his fault, it was the fault of the Newfoundland Government, or it is a misunderstanding. Who cares that hundreds if not thousands of single parents are being gouged for their electrical bills.
In the same manner the Minister has washed his hands of the medical crisis in British Columbia. When confronted with a clear and present violation of the Canada Health Act, did the Minister fight for the rights of Canadians, as did the former Minister, Monique Begin? Did the Minister go to the Government of British Columbia and say, Bill C-50 is a travesty, a violation of the Canada Health Act? Did he say that Bill C-50 must be nipped in the bud? No, Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit, cum Progressive Conservative Government in British Columbia, was aided and abetted by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who has known about this violation of the Canada Health Act for months but has chosen to wash his hands of the issue because he does not have the political guts to go to his colleagues in the provinces and say that this Government is committed to ensuring accessibility under the Canada Health Act; this Government is committed to ensuring accessibility to the child tax credit for all those who need it.
No, Mr. Speaker, when push comes to shove this Government is prepared to kneel and bow and scrape to those provincial Governments who would utilize mechanisms like the child tax credit and the Canada Health Act for their own gain.
This Party introduced the child tax credit and the Canada Health Act, and we are going to fight for Canadians, a job which is not being done by this current Progressive Conservative Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Hamilton-East (Ms. Copps) asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) about the
Adjournment Debate
situation in Newfoundland where people were required to sign over their child tax credit before they could get any help from the Department of Social Services to pay their heating bills.
The Minister answered that officials in his Department had spoken with officials of the Newfoundland Government who had stated very clearly that it was not government policy to ask people to sign over their child tax credit before they could get any financial help. The provincial officials stated that the form signed by Shirley Parsons had never been approved by the Department of Social Services. They regretted what had happened to Mrs. Parsons and informed the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare that she would get the financial assistance needed to pay her heating bill without signing over her child tax credit.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read now a Telex sent to the Minister of National Health and Welfare by the Hon. R. C. Brett, Minister of Social Services in Newfoundland:

This will serve to confirm information provided by my officials during the past few days that it is not the policy of the Newfoundland Department of Social Services to require or request assignments to the Department of Child Tax Credit payments for any purpose. Unfortunately this did occur in error in a very small number of cases. The matter has been corrected and the practice discontinued. The clients concerned have been notified accordingly.
We regret this occurrence and any difficulty this may have caused you.

This convinced the Minister of National Health and Welfare, Mr. Speaker, and should convince all Members that the Newfoundland Government does not require that people sign over their child tax credit before they can receive help.
I want to assure the Hon. Member for Hamilton-East (Ms. Copps) and all the Members, that Newfoundland abides by the terms of the agreement signed with the Federal Government under the Public Assistance Act. I would like to add that the federal Government does not require that the Child Tax Credit be considered as income when determining eligibility to provincial social assistance, and all provinces exclude it totally in their social programs.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-FEDERAL UNIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) PENSION NEGOTIATIONS

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-FEDERAL UNIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) PENSION NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject this evening is Public Service pensions and the promise made by this Government to maintain indexing for the pensions for which public servants have paid premiums and to which they are entitled.
The House will recall that I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), following his statement in the House, to table the so-called agreements he signed with the two largest unions, and I am referring to the Public Service Alliance and the Professional Institute. The President of the Treasury Board refused to do so at the time, saying that if we

May 14, 1985
Adjournment Debate
wanted information, we would have to see the unions, that everything was confidential, and that for the time being it was impossible to judge whether or not there was a good case for settling a problem that has been with us for a long time, that is, four or five very controversial points, including the indexing of pensions.
A few minutes ago, when I was listening to the other speech, at the same time-in the House it becomes second nature-I was reading over a speech I made on December 7, 1982 on the same subject, namely, Bill C-133, which I feel destroyed the indexing of Public Service pensions forever by setting the maximum allowable indexing at 6.5 per cent for one year and 5.5 per cent the following year.
Mr. Speaker, at the time I objected strenuously to this measure, but the fact is that the measure was adopted and I think this injustice should be dealt with very shortly. We were led to believe that an agreement had been reached, that public servants, through their union, had agreed to a remedy and had ratified an agreement they were to submit to management and which would subsequently be ratified by the public servants themselves.
Mr. Speaker, on May 10, after a series of misunderstandings and comments on both sides, both in the press and by spokesmen, by people who we assumed were knowledgeable, we had a rather serious problem, namely, that the unions were saying that what the Minister had read and their interpretation were not the same thing. With respect to pensions, the Minister had said: Unlimited indexing is finished. We are not going to talk about it anymore. We are now going to have an adjustment formula, which I will explain later on, and that is it. He also said: The right to strike was let go in favour of an agreement on other items that were more likely to meet with the general approval of union members. In other words, the right to strike was dropped. The union presidents denied they had dropped the right to strike. They also denied they had agreed to a non-indexed pension plan. In any case, all this created a wave of protest in the press and the media, and finally, last week on May 10, I asked the Minister: Listen, could you put an end to all these misunderstandings and table the agreements in the House? The President of the Treasury Board agreed to do so, and Hon. Members were able to see that quite obviously, the agreements were not what we expected from this Government, which was a settlement that would deal, after so many years, with a problem of major concern to us, and I am referring to pension indexing.
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I have left, I would like to comment on this very important subject of pensions. In the memorandum of agreement signed, as far as I know, by Mr. Donegani for the Professional Institute and by Mr. D. Bean for the Public Service Alliance, it says very clearly:
Premium rates will be set at a level commensurate with the cost of current benefits under the base plan and with the ability to provide full protection against inflation if the economic assumptions on which these rates are based are realized.
Mr. Speaker, that means that the committee will be chaired by an individual allegedly independent of the minister, but who will be nonetheless responsible to him, and who will try to anticipate economic assumptions on inflation interest rates. The system will be based on those factors. How will they manage when, for years, we have been unable to do so with the assistance of so-called professional actuaries, I do not know.
Anyway, here is clause 4 of the agreement:
It is agreed that the present commitment to unlimited indexation will be repealed.
It is clear. For my part, it is the crux of this issue. The unlimited indexation is being repealed.
No. 6. The real level of protection against inflation provided to present and future pensioners will be based on the revenues of the pension fund and determined by the president of the Treasury Board on the recommendations of the management committee.
Whom will the advisory committee advise? The President of the Treasury Board, who will have the final word. This means, Mr. Speaker, that instead of saying: Listen, this thing has been going on for years, it is difficult to explain it, is quite complex and we will start over, both plans are put together. The indexation plan and the pension plan will be placed in a common fund which will be used to purchase long-term bonds bearing current interest and it will be jointly managed not only by the present public servants but also by the 30,000 pensioners who will have their say in the administration of their pension plan.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to end my brief comments this evening by stating that I feel that pension indexation should be maintained. We should be able to negotiate. The minister told us: yes, the door is open, come and see me. However, it is the minister who should act and invite the retired public servants to call at his office to negotiate an agreement which 1 hope will be approved by all and will put an end to a debate which has been going on for 17 years. It would also end the injustice of constantly questioning the future of our pensioners, their means of living, which they have dearly earned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-FEDERAL UNIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) PENSION NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to respond to my Hon. colleague's remarks. I well remember his embarrassment during the six and five debate when he was completely abandoned by the Liberal Party and had to face his constituents. It was very embarrassing for the Member and I appreciate his efforts to try to regain lost ground.
Last Friday, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) indicated a willingness to meet with the union representatives and discuss, further, pension plan reforms and the shape of a new dental plan. I am sure the Hon. Member appreciates that this is one more indication of our willingness as a Government to sit down and consult. I am sure the Hon.
May 14, 1985

Member realizes, as his constituents must be telling him, that there is a much better tone and atmosphere with respect to employer-employee relations under the Conservative Government than that which existed under the previous Liberal Government. Although the Hon. Member cannot admit that because of Party solidarity, he would admit that privately.
On April 17, the President of the Treasury Board, in all good faith, outlined a series of understandings that had been reached, through bargaining on both sides, with the unions representing the Public Service employees. Understandings in principle are worked out and have to be taken back to both sides. They provide a framework within which the specifics can be worked out. They anticipate flexibility, compromise on the details, and most of all they reflect an appreciation that there must be continuing consultation.
Adjournment Debate
I am sure 1 speak for Members of all Parties when I say we regret the events of last week, but we as a Government do not for a minute abandon our hope for continuing constructive joint consultation on the issue of pension reform and a dental plan. Both of these subjects are of importance to present employees. The pension arrangements are naturally important to present employees and retired employees. We see a need to continue these consultations, and I regret that because of the time limit I do not have the opportunity to expand upon these remarks and reply further to my hon. colleague's question.
1 wish to thank the House for this opportunity, Mr. Speaker.
